races.long_description: Representative Barry Moore, a third-term Republican and longtime Trump loyalist, is running for the Senate seat being vacated by Tommy Tuberville, who is running for governor. Mr. Moore’s Democratic opponent, Everett Wess, a former judge and lawyer, is a long shot in deep-red Alabama.

Senator Dan S. Sullivan, a Republican, is trying to hold on to his seat against former Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat. The wild card in the four-person ranked-choice race is the presence of Daniel J. Sullivan, a retiree in a small fishing village who has the same name as the incumbent.
Senator Tom Cotton, a Trump ally and the third-ranking Republican in the chamber, is heavily favored to win a third term. He is facing Hallie Shoffner, a Democrat and sixth-generation farmer.

Senator John Hickenlooper, a moderate incumbent, is running for a second term in a solidly Democratic seat. He faces Mark Baisley, a Republican state senator, and Bob Chew, a Navy veteran and former Republican who is running as an independent.

Senator Chris Coons, a Democrat, is heavily favored to win re-election in a state that Kamala Harris carried by about 15 percentage points two years ago. His Republican challenger is Mike Katz, a doctor who has served in Delaware’s State Senate.

Senator Ashley Moody, the Republican incumbent, is on the Senate ballot for the first time, having been appointed last year to finish Marco Rubio’s term. She faces State Representative Angie Nixon, a progressive who won the Democratic primary in an upset.

Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, is seeking a second term in Georgia, a battleground that both parties this cycle initially considered the toughest for Democrats to hold onto. He is facing Representative Mike Collins, a Republican who won President Trump’s endorsement in the primary.

Senator Jim Risch, 83, a Republican, is heavily favored to win a fourth term in Idaho, a state President Trump carried by more than 36 percentage points in 2024. His toughest challenge comes from Todd Achilles, one of several independents challenging Republicans across the country this year.

Illinois’ open Senate seat, now held by retiring Senator Dick Durbin, a Democrat, is likely to remain blue. Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton, a progressive, is favored to prevail over her Republican opponent, Don Tracy, a former chairman of the state Republican Party.

Representative Ashley Hinson, a Republican, is vying to maintain party control of the seat held by retiring Senator Joni Ernst. Polls have shown her locked in a tight race against Josh Turek, a Democratic state representative, in a state that President Trump won three times.

Senator Roger Marshall, a first-term Republican, is trying to survive an unexpectedly competitive race in deep-red Kansas. He faces Adam Hamilton, a centrist Democrat who has sought to corral farmers’ anger at economic conditions under President Trump.

Representative Andy Barr, a Republican, is running to succeed the retiring Senator Mitch McConnell, whose poor health came under scrutiny in recent months. Mr. Barr faces Charles Booker, a progressive former state lawmaker who has run for the Senate twice before.

Senator Bill Cassidy lost his Republican primary this year after President Trump targeted him for voting to convict him in his second impeachment trial. Now the seat Mr. Cassidy held for over a decade is up for grabs, and Representative Julia Letlow, who is backed by Mr. Trump, is heavily favored to win it over Jamie Davis, a Democratic farmer.
Senator Susan Collins, a Republican, is seeking a sixth term against the Democrat Troy Jackson in the toughest political environment she has faced over her 30-year career.

Senator Ed Markey, 80, a Democrat whose progressive bona fides helped him turn back a much younger challenger in the primary, is running for re-election in a solidly Democratic state. He faces John Deaton, a Republican lawyer and a Marine veteran.

Abdul El-Sayed, a Democratic former public health official, is in a competitive race against former Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican who narrowly lost his Senate bid in 2024. The contest has become a key test for progressives, who are backing El-Sayed.

The race to replace the retiring Senator Tina Smith, a Democrat, pits the state’s lieutenant governor, Peggy Flanagan, a Democrat, against Michele Tafoya, a sports journalist and a first-time candidate. The two have sparred over fraud in statewide programs and rising costs attributed to the Iran war and the Trump administration’s tariff policies.

Scott Colom, a Democratic prosecutor, has mounted an unexpectedly competitive challenge to Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a first-term Republican who has been reliably aligned with President Trump. While Ms. Hyde-Smith is still favored in conservative Mississippi, Mr. Colom would be the first Black senator elected from the state since Reconstruction.

A late withdrawal by the incumbent Republican, Steve Daines, left a Senate seat open in a historically conservative state. Kurt Alme, a Republican backed by President Trump, faces an unusually fractured field after national Democrats and state leaders shifted support toward an independent candidate, Seth Bodnar, instead of the Democrat who won the party’s primary, Alani Bankhead.

Dan Osborn, a mechanic, former union leader and military veteran running as an independent, is challenging Senator Pete Ricketts, a Republican scion of an influential billionaire family with deep ties to Nebraska. To clear the way for Mr. Osborn’s bid, the Democratic primary winner, Cindy Burbank, declined the party’s nomination, potentially consolidating the anti-incumbent vote in the conservative stronghold.

Nearly 20 years ago, John E. Sununu, a Republican, lost his Senate seat to Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat. Now she is retiring, and Mr. Sununu is trying to make a comeback. He is facing Representative Chris Pappas, a low-key Democrat in his fourth term.
Senator Cory Booker, a Democrat and former Newark mayor elected to the Senate in 2013, faces Justin Murphy, a Republican attorney.

Senator Ben Ray Luján, a Democrat, is running for a second term in a solidly blue state against Larry E. Marker, a former oil and gas producer who won the Republican nomination as a write-in candidate.

Roy Cooper, the Democratic former North Carolina governor, and Michael Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman, are competing to succeed Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican who is retiring.

In one of the most expensive and consequential Senate races of this cycle, Senator Jon Husted, a Republican, is facing a challenge from Sherrod Brown, a Democrat. Mr. Brown lost his seat in 2024 after three terms in the Senate.

Markwayne Mullin left the Senate to become secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, and his replacement, Alan Armstrong, is ineligible to seek a full term under state law. Representative Kevin Hern, a Trump ally, is the clear favorite to win the open seat.
Senator Jeff Merkley is running for re-election in a solidly Democratic state. Among his challengers are State Senator David Brock Smith, a Republican, and Gary Lyndon Dye, a Libertarian.

Senator Jack Reed, a Democrat, is seeking a sixth term in a state that has not sent a Republican to the Senate since 2000. He is being challenged by Raymond McKay, a Republican activist who was formerly the network and telecommunications manager for the city of Warwick, R.I.

Senator Darline Graham, the Republican appointed to fill her deceased brother Lindsey Graham’s seat, is running for a full term of her own. Dr. Annie Andrews, a Democrat and a pediatrician, is hoping Ms. Graham’s inexperience and her ties to President Trump can help her flip a seat in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1998.

Senator Mike Rounds, a Republican, is running for a third term in one of the country’s most conservative states. Public polling has been limited, but some surveys have shown him in a closer-than-usual race with Brian Bengs, an independent. The Democratic nominee withdrew from the ballot.

Senator Bill Hagerty, a Trump-backed Republican, is seeking a second term in a state that President Trump won by nearly 30 points in 2024. His opponent, the Democratic environmental justice activist Marquita Bradshaw, previously ran for Senate in 2020 and 2024.

James Talarico, a state legislator, is trying to become the first Democrat in more than three decades to win a statewide election in Texas. He is facing Ken Paxton, the Republican state attorney general, in a race that is one of the most expensive American campaigns ever.
Senator Mark Warner, a Democrat, is seeking a fourth term in a state that is considered solidly blue. He faces Bert Mizusawa, a retired general who easily won the Republican primary.
Senator Shelley Moore Capito is running for a third term in West Virginia, a Republican stronghold. She faces Rachel Fetty Anderson, a lawyer and a Democratic former city councilwoman in Morgantown.

In deep-red Wyoming, the state’s lone at-large House member, Harriet Hageman, is favored to succeed Senator Cynthia Lummis, a Republican, who is retiring after serving one term. Ms. Hageman faces James Byrd, a Democratic former state lawmaker.

Most voters tend to vote early in person, and vote reporting is usually relatively fast. But if a race is very close, it can still take awhile to declare a winner. In 2022, it took until Wednesday afternoon for The A.P. to declare that the top Senate candidates had advanced to a runoff, which was held on Dec. 6.
In 2022 and 2024, about half of the state’s votes were reported by midnight Eastern time on election night, and the count reached 95 percent around 6 a.m. on Wednesday.

In 2024, just under half of voters cast ballots by mail, and it took about two days to report 95 percent of votes statewide. Postmarked ballots must arrive by the fourth day after the election, Nov. 7.

In the past two general elections, 97 percent of the state’s votes were counted by noon Eastern time the day after the election. Counting has sped up since 2020, when it took several days to finish counting mail ballots.

In 2024, 95 percent of the state’s votes were reported by 5 a.m. Eastern time the morning after the election. In some places, absentee ballots are counted at a central facility and reported in large batches.
Most results are typically reported by 1 a.m. Eastern time, and congressional races in recent general elections have been called by The Associated Press on election night.

During the state’s June primaries, this slow process fostered suspicion when two candidates flipped positions five days into vote counting — a phenomenon that is common with election results but usually happens quickly on election night.

The state has long conducted its elections by mail. In 2022 and in 2024, it took about four days to report 95 percent of votes in statewide races. If a race is close, it could take awhile for The A.P. to call a winner.

content.text: House Democrats are watching three key races in Florida to provide them with some early signs of how the night is going: the re-election bids of Representatives Kathy Castor, Jared Moskowitz and Darren Soto. All are Democrats who are vulnerable this year because of Republican redistricting efforts, and their races are likely to be some of the early ones that are called tonight. If they win, Democrats said they expected more good news to follow through the night.

The first votes out of Indiana’s Fifth Congressional District show an advantage for Democrats. If reporting patterns are consistent with the 2024 presidential election, that first drop is early vote. In 2024, Kamala Harris won the first drop in Hamilton County, primarily consisting of early votes, by two percentage points, before ultimately losing the county by six. Tonight, J.D. Ford, the Democrat, is winning the first drop in Hamilton County by 27 points.
Indiana Fifth Congressional District Election Results ›

Statewide race calls won’t come in Florida until 8 p.m. Eastern at the earliest. The state, where polls close at 7 p.m. local time, is mostly in the Eastern time zone except for the Panhandle, which is on Central time. The Associated Press will wait until all polls are closed across the state before declaring winners in the statewide races.

The polls at Henry Ford High School, which is in a predominantly Black neighborhood in Detroit, have been active all day with voters of all ages. Many are casting ballots for the first time, volunteers here said.

“They’re coming in like crazy, all of these cars out here on the streets, and the parking lot is full,” said Diane Roberts, 75, a poll worker who has helped run precincts in the area for the last four election cycles. “I’ve never seen anything like this.”
Democrats have been counting on high Black turnout to win the state’s competitive race for Senate. Republicans, too, have made efforts to court Black voters this year.

Turnout has been high in general, but in Florida it is running roughly on par with the 2024 presidential election, and Republicans are winning Election Day votes by a nearly two-to-one margin. The result? While Republicans led registered Democrats by just two percentage points in the advance vote — their lowest such advantage in years — they now lead by nearly nine points statewide. In 2024, they had an 11-point advantage. Of course, party registration can’t tell us much about persuasion, and any Democratic victory in Florida, where Republican numbers have surged in recent years, would come from winning over a large number of Republicans and independents.

content.text: I’m in Anchorage, Alaska, where a handful of large signs on street corners warn voters that one House candidate, Eric Hafner, is not who he seems. Hafner is running as a Democrat but is also an inmate in federal prison whom Republicans have propped up before, and Democrats are worried that he will split votes with the independent candidate they’re backing, Bill Hill.
It’s another example of ballot stacking, the strategy that has
made headlines
after
The New York Times reported
that aides for Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate for Senate, were involved in recruiting a second Dan Sullivan into the race against the incumbent Republican senator, also named Dan Sullivan.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic minority leader, just spoke briefly to reporters, projecting confidence about his party’s chances of winning the House. Still, he would not say whether he planned to call President Trump once the results were in, and he would not make projections on how big a margin Democrats might have next year.

He said he was particularly focused on watching the results in Kentucky’s Sixth District, a traditionally safe Republican district that is in play this year and could give a sense of what direction the night is taking. “Today’s vote numbers all across the country are strong,” he said. “We’ll look at Virginia, we’ll look at Pennsylvania, as two critical states, as well as North Carolina.” He said he was confident that members would be seated on Jan. 3 and that there would be a “peaceful transfer of power,” and he said that his first call after results were in would be to his mother.

Polls have closed in eastern Kentucky, the first of the night. Pre-election polls in the state showed Andy Barr, the Republican candidate running to replace Senator Mitch McConnell, leading Charles Booker, the Democratic candidate, by around nine percentage points. While that is a significant margin, President Trump won the state by more than 30 points in 2024.

For the first hour after polls start to close at 6 p.m. Eastern, Kentucky will be one of the two states reporting results. One of the earliest races to watch will be in the state’s Sixth Congressional District, where
polling

has been sparse. The only publicly released surveys have come from Zach Dembo, the Democratic nominee, or Democratic-affiliated organizations, making it likely that results are being released selectively. Still, Dembo has led in these polls since late July, including by more than five percentage points in each of the four most recent surveys.
The race remains highly uncertain, but the results may offer one of the first indications of how Democrats are performing in red districts; President Trump won the Sixth by 16 points in 2024.
Kentucky Sixth Congressional District Election Results ›

President Trump is set to start hosting an election watch party in the East Room later this evening. His Truth Social feed suggests he’s been watching Fox News, along with other coverage, none of which has indicated that a good night is coming for the bulk of his party.
Polls in South Carolina
show a surprisingly tight race. In a state that Donald Trump won by about 18 percentage points in 2024, the latest
Times/Siena poll

shows Darline Graham, the Republican senator, running neck-and-neck with Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee. Graham, who was recently appointed to the Senate after her brother, Lindsey Graham, died earlier this year, has been ahead by a narrow margin in many of the other polls.

In Juneau, Alaska, Elizabeth Thomas said Republican suggestions that the state’s top-four, ranked-choice ballots or the placement of two candidates named Dan Sullivan might confuse people were overblown. It took her just a few minutes at the Alaska State Museum to vote for Mary Peltola.

“People here know how to do it,” she said. “It’s not complicated.” Thomas, 43, works in natural resource management and said she voted for Peltola because she is part Alaska Native and agrees with her on many issues, especially environmental ones.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and minority leader, just arrived at the hotel in Washington where volunteers are phone banking, to thank them for their work. “What you all have represented throughout the last two years, which have been incredibly difficult, gives us all hope and inspiration that we are going to be able to bring about a brighter future,” he told a few dozen young volunteers who were making calls. “We’re on the brink of a dramatic change of direction in this country,” he said. “We’re on the brink of Democrats taking back control of the House of Representatives.”

content.text: Representative Suzan DelBene of Washington State, the chair of the House Democrats campaign arm, told me earlier today that she is confident Democrats will win the House majority but does not expect to have enough races called tonight to know for sure. “I’m a West Coaster so I know our numbers won’t come in until closer to 11,” DelBene said. “We might have to wait a while later tonight before all the results come in.”
Polls in Florida
show Ashley Moody, the incumbent Republican senator, with the lead over Angie Nixon in the Florida Senate race. A
Times/Siena poll
from mid-October showed Moody ahead by six percentage points. Other polls show a similar lead for the senator.
The race for governor looks quite a bit tighter than the Senate race. Still,
polls show
Byron Donalds, the Republican, with an edge over David Jolly, the Democratic nominee. The Times/Siena poll found Donalds with a four-percentage-point edge.
I’m in Bethlehem, Pa., where a hotly contested House race in Pennsylvania’s Seventh District has kept poll workers busy with a steady stream of voters all day.

Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, told reporters at the White House on Tuesday afternoon that he did not send federal immigration agents to polling sites today, which had been a widespread concern among civil rights and immigrant advocacy groups leading up to the election.

I’m at Ohio State University in Columbus, where volunteers are stationed around campus trying to make sure students have cast their ballots in one of this year’s most closely watched Senate races. Polls have shown Sherrod Brown, a Democrat and former senator, has some of the best odds in the country of flipping a Republican Senate seat — but in order to do so, he needs progressives like many of the students on campus to vote.

At the student union, one of the polling locations on campus, one student just told me she had waited an hour to vote for Democrats. “This year I was really big on affordability,” said Abigail Clayton, 19. She expected the line to grow even longer this evening.“I just know that people on campus don’t wake up until 2 p.m.,“ she said.

All eyes are on Texas tonight, where it looks as if the state’s record-breaking number of early voters are being followed by robust turnout on Election Day. In Harris County, one of the state’s most populous, around 180,000 Election Day votes had been cast as of 3 p.m. Eastern. That number may be below what some had imagined in a year in which hundreds of millions of dollars were spent on the Senate race, but it is not far removed from the 200,000 or so who had voted at the same point in the 2024 presidential election. If current trends continue, overall turnout in the state could exceed 10 million votes, which would be more than what was seen in the last two midterm elections.

For being a purple state, North Carolina has had a relatively quiet midterm year largely because of its sleepy Senate race between former Gov. Roy Cooper, a moderate Democrat, and Michael Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman. Consultants of all political stripes and virtually all polls agree that Cooper, who has never lost a race, is heavily favored.

But several Republicans and party activists in the state fear that Whatley’s weak candidacy could drag down the rest of the ticket. Among their concerns is possibly losing both chambers of the legislature, which would give Democrats full control of the state for the first time since 2010.

content.text: For each of the seats up for election today, the time it takes to project a winner will depend on two factors: how fast the state counts its votes, and how close the race is. Here’s how quickly the results came in 2024 for the six competitive Senate races rated as tossups by the Cook Political Report:

Speaking with reporters in frigid temperatures after voting at the Alaska Zoo in Anchorage, Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican in a tight race, kept his closing message focused on the recent revelations that aides of his Democratic opponent, Mary Peltola, were involved in recruiting a second Dan Sullivan onto the ballot. “We are witnessing the biggest election cheating scandal in the history of the state of Alaska,” Sullivan said.
Several voters I’ve spoken to at polling places around Columbia, S.C., today have brought up a name that is not on the ballot: Senator Lindsey Graham, who
died in July

. Some of them are extending the good will they felt toward Graham to his sister, Darline, who was appointed to fill out his term and is now the Republican nominee in a close race for the same Senate seat. Others argued that the situation reeked of nepotism.

“I would rather see someone totally incompetent, who doesn’t know what they’re doing, get in there and learn her job rather than deal with someone who is from a political background,” said Mia Lynch, 59, who lives in Columbia, S.C. and does not consider herself a supporter of either political party. She said she saw Dr. Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee in the race, as “the lesser of two evils.”
A small group held signs encouraging voting outside of the Beaches Regional Library polling site in Neptune Beach, Fla. “Trump is still going to be president
but we can vote for a check on his power, his corruption, by voting for Democrats right now,” said Melissa Strandhagen, who was holding a sign that read “Constitution over party.”

Speaking to CNN just now, Representative Mike Lawler, the Hudson Valley Republican defending his seat, said the problems with vote counting in Westchester County were “very frustrating,” but he said anyone who votes today will have their ballots counted. He said that A.D.A. compliant ballot-counting machines were being set up right now at election sites, so ballots can be processed. Ballots that were cast but not accepted this morning, he said, will be transported by police escort to the county board of the elections heaquarters and counted under the observation of lawyers from both parties.

He noted that there would be 10 machines at the board of elections headquarters, and each will be able to process about 2,000 ballots per hour. This process, he hoped, will rebut any complaints or assertions of conspiracy to tip the election in either his or his opponent’s favor. “It’s going to take a few hours,” he said. “We expect to have results certainly into the wee hours of tomorrow morning.”

content.text: The final tally of spending by Trump super PACs in the 2026 midterms is about $374 million, according to a tally of filings with the Federal Election Commission. That includes about $38 million on the Senate race in Texas; $36 million in Michigan; and $29 million in Ohio. A Trump nonprofit called Securing American Greatness also made $10.5 million in donations to other super PACs through Oct. 14, pushing the total bill for the Trump operation’s midterm spending to at least $384 million. President Trump wrote on Truth Social last month that “I would have spent, or will be spending, over 400 Million Dollars by Election Day.”

As voters continue to head to the polls, election workers have started to process absentee ballots in Milwaukee. Workers are paired across political affiliations, often with a Republican and a Democrat working together.

Two House races in particular are top-of-mind for people nervous about the rapid spread of artificial intelligence. One of them is in Colorado’s Eighth District, where Manny Rutinel, a Democrat with longstanding ties to the so-called effective altruist movement, is trying to beat the Republican incumbent, Gabe Evans.

The other is in San Francisco, where Scott Wiener, a state legislator who has long been vocal about artificial intelligence safety issues, is in a surprisingly competitive Democrat-versus-Democrat race to succeed Nancy Pelosi. Those are the two races that will be watched most closely tonight by A.I.-safety advocates.

Control of the Senate is at stake on Tuesday. To win a majority, Democrats would need to flip four seats and hold all the ones they currently represent. It’s a challenge because the road runs through reliable Republican states, but Democrats have a chance because of President Trump’s unpopularity. I worked with some of my colleagues to come up with a way for you to try your hand at deciding the key races.
Give it a shot

The Senate race in Texas has focused on the two major candidates: the Republican, Ken Paxton, and the Democrat, James Talarico. But there is a third name on the ballot in Texas: a libertarian candidate, Ted Brown. Brown, 66, ran for Senate two years ago and received about 260,000 votes, more than 2 percent of ballots cast.

In an interview, Brown told me that he was aware he could be a spoiler this time around, if the race is close, and that he expected to draw more votes from Paxton than from Talarico. “I didn’t run to be a spoiler, I just ran to promote liberty,” he said. “If the Republicans lose because of it, it just means they should nominate better candidates.”
Polls in Iowa
have depicted an extremely tight Senate race. The final
Times/Siena poll

showed Josh Turek, the Democratic nominee, with a one-percentage-point edge over Representative Ashley Hinson. In a state President Trump won by more than 13 percentage points in 2024, Hinson, the Republican nominee, led in just over half of the polls released in the month before the election. But the race has been consistently close, with neither candidate leading by more than four percentage points in any poll since late September.

Lewiston, Maine, has a large Somali population, and its mayor, Carl Sheline, said last week that Somali voters had been “harassed nonstop by political provocateurs and agitators all throughout early voting.” On Election Day, Isha Dagane, 28, and some of her Somali friends were keeping an eye on one of the city’s polling sites. Dagane recalled President Trump’s
bashing of Somali immigrants
, adding, “Everybody should feel welcome.”

On a day that will be watched closely for the future influence and viability of the progressive movement, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s campaign released a detailed memo highlighting her activities over the past two years. Summing up her endorsements and campaign rallies, and the money she has raised for other candidates, the memo ends with an unusual acknowledgement of the 2028 buzz surrounding her.

“In the coming days and weeks, much will be discussed about the future of the Democratic Party and 2028,” the campaign memo reads. “You may be asked whether you support her running for president or for Senate in New York or staying in the House of Representatives. We’d recommend you rely on the details of this memo and answer that Rep. Ocasio-Cortez will continue to do what she’s always done: look for ways to do the most good for the most people.”

At the Golden Triangle Branch Library in Fort Worth, signs posted outside the building and at the entrance informed voters that it was no longer a polling location. Earlier this year, the Republican-led Tarrant County Commissioners Court eliminated more than 90 polling locations, which Democrats said would mostly affect Black and Hispanic neighborhoods.

Amber Johnson, the library branch’s customer service supervisor, said that although Golden Triangle had stopped serving as a polling location before the county’s recent decision, at least five people an hour were arriving, confused about why they could no longer vote there.

It’s nearly 80 degrees here in Columbia, S.C., where Gov. Henry McMaster just left the senior center that serves as his polling place. A Republican, he appointed Darline Graham to the Senate in July, after the death of her brother, Lindsey, and said he was confident that she would prevail in her extraordinarily close Senate race.

If the candidates aren’t motivating New Hampshire voters to go the polls, maybe Gronk can do the job. Rob Gronkowski, the former star of the N.F.L.’s New England Patriots and Tampa Bay Buccaneers, was spotted outside New Hampshire polling places today, urging people to vote. “It doesn’t matter what party you’re voting for,” he said, according to a
video clip
posted by WHDH, a Boston news station. “It just matters that you’re voting.”

It’s still early, but Election Day turnout looks strong for Republicans in Florida. They are outpacing registered Democrats by roughly a two-to-one margin in ballots cast today — similar to their performance four years ago. However, Republicans saw a narrower lead in advance voting this year, leading by about two percentage points compared to roughly six in 2022.
The majority of Florida’s votes are typically cast before Election Day, making today’s turnout less representative than it is in a state like Ohio, which is also seeing strong in-person turnout.
After casting a ballot voters often receive stickers, which have different styles throughout the country.

An office of Senator Susan Collins of Maine, a vulnerable Republican, was vandalized last night, according to her aides. The words “Blood on her Hands,” were scrawled in red on the sidewalk outside the office in Biddeford, Maine, according to images provided by a Collins spokeswoman.

The office, outside Portland, was also vandalized about a month ago. Katie Brown, Collins’s chief of staff, said in a statement that the episode was an attempt to “intimidate the Senator and her staff,” and that it was “disturbing, but not effective.” Biddeford was the site
of the killing of an immigrant by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement
agent in July, and immigration policy has been a focus of Collins’s race against Troy Jackson, a Democrat.

To win a majority in the Senate, Democrats would need to win three of the six competitive races rated as tossups by the Cook Political Report. Republicans must win four tossup races to retain control of the Senate.
